before.exact_excerpt: The quantum algorithm has two tasks. It first produces a short list of columns that is likely to contain the winning column, if there is one. It then checks the columns in that list. Both tasks must have a fixed query bound on every input, including inputs on which some of the Forrelation promises fail. This requirement determines the amplification procedure and the comparison rule below.

after.exact_excerpt: The algorithm first produces a short list likely to contain the winning column, then checks the listed columns. Its central calculation is a drift identity: complementary comparison probabilities make the total surviving weight fall by at least half in expectation, while a true winner retains almost all its weight until it is selected. This works even if the other columns compare cyclically or have meaningless decoded addresses. Exact local verification subsequently rejects incorrect certificates. Both the search and the verification have a fixed query cap on every input, including inputs outside all the partial-function promises.

before.exact_excerpt:
We compare the real process with the ideal one on a common probability space. As long as their lists agree, let \(f(L)\) be the failure probability of the amplified sampler for that list. If \(W>0\), independently choose a possible ideal next pivot with distribution \(w_i/W\), and a Bernoulli variable that reports failure with probability \(f(L)\). On nonfailure, give both processes the chosen pivot. On failure, stop the real process and continue the ideal one with its ordinary transitions. This has the correct marginal distribution for each process: the real sampler's successful probability for pivot \(i\) is exactly \((1-f(L))w_i/W\). Independence here is a way to construct the coupling from that law; it is not an additional property demanded of the implementation.

after.exact_excerpt: Suppose $s$ is dominant. At an agreed history of length at most $T$ before $s$ is selected, the preceding lower bound gives $W>1/2$. Thus $W/m\geq1/(2m)$, and $f(L)\leq\varepsilon$. For each of the at most $T$ stages, condition on the event that there has been no earlier disagreement and $s$ has not yet appeared. The conditional chance of a new disagreement is at most $\varepsilon$. Multiplying by the probability of the conditioning event and summing over the stages gives a total at most $T\varepsilon$. No independence among these stage failures is needed.

before.exact_excerpt: There are useful precedents for the three steps of generating candidates, comparing them, and checking a certificate. Ben-David and Kothari use this organization in their quantum certificate separation [BenDavidKothari2026, Lemma 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15063). Quantum minimum finding provides another example of repeatedly searching among candidates [DurrHoyer1996, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9607014). Its comparisons come from a total order. Finding a king in a fixed tournament also has a quantum algorithm using a square root number of vertices, up to logarithmic factors [MandeParaasharSaurabh2023, Theorem 4.4](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.FSTTCS.2023.30). Here a comparison is a quantum experiment whose winning probability can be any real number in the unit interval. In particular, an input outside the Forrelation promises need not determine a reliable orientation of each edge. We therefore prove the probabilistic tournament statement needed for this setting.

after.exact_excerpt: The organization into candidate generation, comparison and certificate checking also appears in Ben-David and Kothari [BDK2026, §3, Lemma 5, pp. 3–5]. Dürr and Høyer's minimum-finding algorithm uses ordered table values and a decreasing rank [DH1999, Theorem 1 and Lemmas 1–2, pp. 1–2]. Mande, Paraashar and Saurabh give a quantum algorithm for finding a king with exact edge-direction queries [MPS2023, Theorem 19, §4, pp. 30:11–30:13]. These are antecedents and comparisons; the fractional-weight argument here is the one in OpenAI's Proposition 3.2. In particular, the available comparisons need not be bounded-error evaluations of any fixed orientation.
